newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean car makers eye exports to ease oversupply.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean car makers eye exports to ease oversupply.

text.p: South Korean car makers have bet on exports to overcome excess capacity and slowing sales at home, but the road to profitability is riddled with potholes, analysts and company officials said on Thursday.
The biggest question facing Korea's car industry, the world's fifth largest, may be whether the world wants or needs the cars it is now churning out at a rate of four million a year.

Capacity of Korea's three leading auto makers is scheduled to top six million vehicles annually by 2000. Domestic sales stood at 1.64 million cars last year and are not expected to increase much this year.
Worldwide car production is set to double to about 100 million vehicles annually by 2010 with the main sales increases seen in developing countries.
"Over-capacity, if any, will prompt a shakeout in the industry. Survivors will come out stronger and will compete better in the world market," said Kim Woo-choong, chairman of the Daewoo Group.

Kim's comments came earlier this week in a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the opening of third-ranked Daewoo Motor Co Ltd's newest car assembly complex. It adds 300,000 vehicles to Daewoo's annual capacity, bringing its total to 1.6 million.
Analysts said Korean car makers had no choice but to export.

"Our exports account for about two percent of the world's demand. Emerging markets, such as China and Southeast Asian countries, will provide room for South Korean producers," said Nam Seung-soo, an analyst at Daishin Economic Research Institute.
Korean companies have set an overseas sales goal of four million units in 2000. This year's target is 1.5 million.
Analysts said it would not be easy for South Korean companies to make internationally viable models.

"The world's leading companies are also actively rushing into emerging markets to claim a bigger slice of market share and they will become more reluctant to provide technology to Korean makers," said Yang Dong-ki of Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
Korean car makers remain dependent to varying degrees on foreign technology.
Analysts said low technology standards among the nation's part suppliers and high labour costs would continue dragging down the industry.
Ahn Suk-woo, spokesman for the Kia Group, said Kia would focus on the 1.5 litre engine market. "That segment is where South Korean makers can compete best," he said.
Analysts said market diversification would boost exports.
South Korea depended on the United States for more than 80 percent of its total car exports in 1988, but now the U.S. share of Korean exports is less than 20 percent.
A slumping economy has led Korean consumers to cut spending on durable goods, including cars.
Stockpiled vehicles rose to 180,000 at the end of March, compared to the acceptable level of 120,000, analysts said. Hyundai Motor Co cut production.
Exports were hurt by the weak yen which makes Japanese products less expensive in overseas markets, analysts said.

"Current difficulties made us review our car industry. In two or three years, I believe, we can emerge stronger and much healthier," Hyundai Motor chairman Chung Mong-gyu told Reuters at the '97 Seoul Motor Show.
